says: Opus supervises a Haiku worker; Opus repairs in the same session
lead: You supervise Haiku workers: plan the work, split it into the steps you judge best, and start as many `haiku-worker` subagents as you decide, one per step and several at once where steps are independent; check what each returns, and do a step yourself only when that is quicker than explaining it; the result is yours.

findings: src/sim.js hit() misses grazing collisions: with AI off, player at (0,1.449,0) and computer at (10,0,180), firing then stepping 0.7 seconds leaves computer health at 100 despite contact.
src/sim.js fly() reflects the wrong wall face: firing from (-10.2,10) heading 0 teleports the shell from z=10 to z=8 without reversing its x velocity, then removes it on the next step.
src/view.js resize() moves the camera beyond its fixed 200-unit far plane at a 200×1200 window size, making the arena and tanks disappear.

src/sim.js:93 misses exact shell–tank contact because hit() uses < instead of <=: with AI disabled, player at (0,1.45) heading 0 and computer at (10,0), firing and stepping 0.75 seconds leaves computer health at 100 and the shell alive instead of dealing 25 damage and removing it; add a tangency regression test.

src/sim.js fly() handles only one wall contact per step: firing from the valid position (18.8, 13.8) at heading 45 leaves a shell outside the arena at (19.75, 15.108) after one step instead of resolving its second wall contact.
src/sim.js fly() discards the remaining movement after a bounce, violating the specified shell speed: firing from (0, 0) at heading 0 leaves the shell at x=19.75 after 73 steps instead of x=19.65.
The 31-test suite passes, but no tests exercise shells passing through each other or the canvas following browser resize, both implemented behaviours required by the spec.
